title: The Verdict of the Fens Anew
premise: Jude Halloran left the force after a case she was never allowed to close, and now the case has found her: a confession letter naming three men in the drowning of a girl in the fens thirty years ago, mailed the day after the last witness's funeral. As the statute of limitations ticks down, Jude discovers her late husband was one of the letter's possible authors and that the town's beloved founding families built their fortunes on silence. Following alibis that were rehearsed before she was born, she must choose between prosecuting the truth and protecting the one innocent person left who trusts her. In the end, Jude stages a public reckoning at the fen itself — not a trial, but a verdict delivered by the whole town — and walks away from both justice and the law, keeping only the bookshop and the truth.
about_author: Mirabel Hartwell is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent two decades transcribing other people's confessions before writing her own stories. She lives near the East Anglian marshes, where she collects tide tables and unsolved cases.

chapters.title: Postmarked Grief
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Three days after old Tom Ellery's funeral, Jude finds an unsigned confession among the bookshop's returns bin, postmarked the day after the burial. It names a drowned girl, Ada Voss, and three men. The emotional beat is dread disguised as routine — Jude recognizes the handwriting style of someone trained to write reports.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Silence
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. She pulls her private files on the Voss case, closed as accidental drowning in 1994, and realizes every key witness has died or moved away except one: Ellery himself, whose funeral started this. Beat: cold clarity hardening into obsession as she maps thirty years of convenient deaths.

chapters.title: Three Men, One Tide
chapters.summary: Jude interviews the surviving suspects' descendants under the guise of buying rare books: magistrate's son Aldous Crane, farmer Bram Tewson, and the third name smudged beyond reading. Each alibi is word-for-word identical, learned like scripture. Beat: unease — these are rehearsed lies, and rehearsed by whom?

chapters.title: What My Husband Kept
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, flashback-woven. Clearing her late husband Daniel's desk, she finds his old police notebook with the same date circled — he was the responding officer in 1994 and wrote a report that contradicts the official one. Beat: betrayal; the man she loved may have buried the case, or been silenced.

chapters.title: The Statute Burns Down
chapters.summary: Jude's POV with interludes from young Ada's diary (found in Ellery's effects). A lawyer confirms prosecution expires in six weeks. Someone ransacks the bookshop but takes only paper. Beat: acceleration — Jude is no longer investigating; she is being hunted by someone cleaning up.

chapters.title: Bram's Confession
chapters.summary: Dual POV: Jude and Bram Tewson, dying of cancer, who admits he held the lantern that night but swears the smudged third name belongs to a woman — Ada's own aunt, who arranged it all to protect the family's land deal. Beat: pity curdling into horror; the victim's family authored the cover-up.

chapters.title: The Letter Writer
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Handwriting analysis and a printer's plate hidden in Ellery's coffin flowers reveal the confession was written by Ellery over decades — a serial confession, mailed to himself, finally released by his daughter Ruth. Ruth confronts Jude: publish it and destroy the town, or bury it and become complicit. Beat: moral vertigo.

chapters.title: Alibi, Rehearsed
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. She reconstructs the night: the identical alibis were coached by the aunt, and Daniel's altered report bought the town its silence — then cost him his life when he tried to recant. Beat: grief transformed; her husband's death five years ago was no accident, and the statute clock is a trap.

chapters.title: Verdict at the Fen
chapters.summary: Jude's POV climax. On the statute's final day, she gathers the town at the drained fen where Ada's belongings still lie, reads the confession aloud, and names every hand — including the dead aunt's and the living Ruth's choice to tell. The crowd must decide; the Cranes walk out, but the majority stays standing in the rain. Beat: catharsis without triumph.

chapters.title: Shelved Under Truth
chapters.summary: Jude's POV resolution. No arrests come — the law expires — but the town renames the footpath for Ada Voss, and Ruth donates Ellery's papers to the bookshop. Jude shelves them between fiction and fact, where they belong. Final beat: quiet peace; some verdicts are rendered outside any courtroom, and she can live inside hers.
